subject: Interconnect evaluation: edge proxy vs interface endpoint vs IPsec

Hi Irene / Karthik,

Thanks for the quick intro call last week. Per our internal architecture review, we need a short written recommendation from Redwood on the best onramp pattern for our Private deployment pilot. Constraints:
- Latency target: p95 <25ms from our app tier to inference (US-WEST region)
- Security: data-in-transit must be mTLS + customer-managed KMS for keys; we also need minimal internet egress from our VPC (audit requirement)
- Operational: we prefer a single, predictable hostname (no surprise DNS changes) and a path that works across our multi-account org
- Cost: sensitive to sustained per-GB egress; prefer a solution that avoids perpetual cross-account data transfer spikes

Can you summarize tradeoffs between VPC peering, PrivateLink (interface endpoints), and a site-to-site IPsec VPN? Also include a suggested PoC plan and rough owner/time estimate.

If helpful, our NetOps lead (cc'd) can share current VPC topology.

Thanks,
Samir

Subject: Re: Interconnect evaluation: options (peering / endpoint / s2s VPN)

Samir — thanks, this is helpful. High-level recommendation up front: PrivateLink (interface endpoints) for primary traffic, with an IPsec site-to-site VPN as a documented fallback for on-prem or cross-cloud failover. VPC peering is attractive only when both VPCs are within compatible accounts/regions and you control route tables end-to-end; for your multi-account setup it quickly becomes operationally brittle.

Quick tradeoffs (short):
- PrivateLink (interface endpoint):
  • Security: strong — traffic terminates at an endpoint service, supports endpoint policy and enforced egress control.
  • Latency: typically slightly higher than same-account peering (additional ENI hop) but still well within p95 20–30ms for US-WEST in our tests.
  • Cross-account: designed for it; supports per-endpoint access controls and private DNS.
  • Ops: scales via endpoint ENIs and NLBs on our side; easier to rotate certificates and audit.
  • Cost: per-ENI/hour + per-GB data processing charges — predictable but not free.

- VPC Peering:
  • Security: simple L3 connectivity; no managed endpoint to gate access (requires strict route/filter discipline).
  • Latency: lowest (best-case) when peering in-region & same cloud provider — minimal hops.
  • Cross-account: supported but many vendors have limits (peering across multiple accounts / transitive peering is painful).
  • Ops: higher blast radius for misconfig; NAT / egress control can be tricky if you need to restrict internet-bound traffic.
  • Cost: usually just data transfer costs; no per-endpoint charges.

- Site-to-site IPsec VPN:
  • Security: good when using customer-managed keys; can terminate in your on-prem or in a cloud VPN gateway.
  • Latency: higher and more variable (depends on Internet path). Not ideal for strict low-p95 latencies.
  • Ops: good fall-back for on-prem or hybrid sites; needs BGP (recommended) to handle failover.
  • Cost: modest for tunnel endpoints; bandwidth caps and throughput limits can matter with heavy traffic.

Suggested PoC (3–4 weeks):
1) Week 0–1: Configure PrivateLink endpoint (test account) + sample workload to measure p50/p95. Owner: Redwood infra eng (Karthik).
2) Week 1–2: Configure an IPsec VPN into a small on-prem VM / cloud VPN GW to validate failover path and BGP convergence. Owner: Acme NetOps + Redwood (Monica).
3) Week 2–3: Load test (1k rps burst, steady 100 rps) and collect token-level latency & per-token cost. Owner: joint.
4) Week 3–4: Define runbook + monitoring alerts + procurement checkpoint (if per-endpoint charges exceed threshold).

I've attached a short decision memo and a schematic we can iterate on. Can we book a 45-minute tech session tomorrow to walk the team through?

Best,
Irene Choi
Senior Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference

Samir — adding a few operational details that often tip the decision:

> On Mon, Nov 9, 2026 at 11:30 AM Irene Choi <irene@redwood.com> wrote:
> > High-level recommendation up front: PrivateLink (interface endpoints) for primary traffic, with an IPsec site-to-site VPN as a documented fallback for on-prem or cross-cloud failover.

Operational notes:
- DNS & service discovery: PrivateLink + private DNS gives you a stable hostname without public DNS changes. With peering you'd need to manage cross-VPC DNS resolution (Route53 Resolver / conditional forwarders).
- NAT & egress restrictions: If you need to eliminate internet egress, PrivateLink helps because traffic hits the service endpoint rather than traversing the public internet. Peering can still allow egress if route tables / NACLs are misconfigured.
- KV cache/keepalive behavior: our inference runtime uses long-lived KV cache flows; PrivateLink sessions to an NLB-backed service maintain TCP connections via ENIs — ensure endpoint ENI limits are sized. For high-concurrency low-latency workloads, we typically recommend endpoint warm pools on our fleet side.
- Cross-region / cross-account scale: PrivateLink scales well across accounts; peering across regions is vendor-specific and often more steps.
- Observability: PrivateLink gives clearer per-endpoint metrics (connection counts, bytes) vs peering where you must instrument VPC flow logs.

Cost/estimate: ballpark for your pilot (monthly):
- PrivateLink endpoint (single AZ proof): endpoint hourly + ~£/USD 0.01/GB data processing (estimate depends on cloud).
- Peering: primarily data transfer costs — cheaper per-GB inside the same region but less control.
- VPN: cheap for low throughput, but if you need sustained high throughput the gateway charges and potential egress costs add up.

Recommended MAP (Mutual Action Plan) items (owners & rough duration):
1) Schedule tech call + share topology (Samir) — 1 week.
2) Redwood create PrivateLink service + temporary test creds (Irene / Karthik) — 1 week.
3) Acme deploy endpoint & test connectivity + perf (Samir NetOps) — 1 week.
4) Load test & cost measurement (joint) — 1 week.
5) Sign off / procurement gating (Acme procurement + Redwood sales) — 1–2 weeks depending on pricing negotiation.

I'll join the tech call. I can also push a short script to validate p95 tokens per client region.

—Karthik
